attribution.sky: Star, constellation, deep-sky and Milky Way data: d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD-3-Clause), stars from the Hipparcos catalogue (ESA 1997).
attribution.galactic: Galactic objects: galactic-map.html CATALOG, extracted at build time.

galactic.name: Sagittarius A*
galactic.desc: Supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. Mass ~4.15 million M☉. Directly imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in May 2022, revealing the characteristic crescent of emission and shadow predicted by general relativity. Surrounded by the S-star cluster whose orbits provide the most direct gravitational proof of its mass. Unlike M87, Sgr A* is a quiescent LLAGN with no bright relativistic jet — only faint, contested ~15–30 ly candidate outflows seen at radio (Brunthaler+ 2018, Royster+ 2019) and X-ray (Li+ 2013) wavelengths.

galactic.name: Proxima Centauri
galactic.desc: The nearest individual star to the Sun at 4.244 ly. A red dwarf flare star loosely bound to the α Centauri system. Hosts Proxima b, a potentially habitable exoplanet, and Proxima d.
props: Proxima b, c, d (b in HZ)

galactic.name: α Centauri A/B
galactic.desc: Nearest star system to the Sun at 4.37 ly (excluding Proxima). Binary: α Cen A (G2V, 1.1 M☉) + α Cen B (K1V, 0.9 M☉). Loosely accompanied by Proxima Centauri.

galactic.name: Barnard's Star
galactic.desc: Second-nearest star system (5.96 ly). Has the highest proper motion of any star — 10.3 arcsec/yr. Will be the nearest star to Earth in ~9,800 CE. Candidate exoplanet Barnard's Star b reported but disputed.

galactic.name: Wolf 359
galactic.desc: Extremely dim red dwarf — third-faintest star known. One of the least massive stars capable of nuclear fusion. Famous from Star Trek as the site of the Battle of Wolf 359.

galactic.name: Sirius
galactic.desc: Brightest star in Earth's night sky. Binary: Sirius A (A1V, 2.06 M☉) + Sirius B (DA2 white dwarf, 1.018 M☉).

galactic.name: ε Eridani
galactic.desc: Nearby K-type star with confirmed debris disk. Long-time SETI target (Project Ozma, 1960). Age ~800 Myr — relatively young.

galactic.name: Procyon
galactic.desc: Eighth-brightest star. F5 subgiant with a white dwarf companion (Procyon B). The binary pair orbit each other every ~40.8 years.

galactic.name: τ Ceti
galactic.desc: Sun-like star at 11.91 ly. One of two stars targeted by Project Ozma (1960). Candidate multi-planet system with up to 5 exoplanets.

galactic.name: 61 Cygni
galactic.desc: "Piazzi's Flying Star" — first star to have its parallax measured (Bessel, 1838). Binary K-dwarf pair separated by ~84 AU. High proper motion star.

galactic.name: Altair
galactic.desc: Brightest star in Aquila. Rotates so rapidly (8.9 hr) it is noticeably oblate — equatorial radius ~20% larger than polar. One of the vertices of the Summer Triangle.

galactic.name: TRAPPIST-1
galactic.desc: Ultra-cool red dwarf hosting 7 Earth-sized planets, at least 3 in the habitable zone (e, f, g). Among the most studied systems for atmospheric characterization with JWST.
props: 7 Earth-sized; e, f, g in HZ

galactic.name: Vega
galactic.desc: Fifth-brightest star. Rapidly rotating — equatorial diameter 19% larger than polar. Once the pole star (~12,000 BCE) and will be again (~13,700 CE).

galactic.name: Fomalhaut
galactic.desc: Solitary bright star in Piscis Austrinus with a famous dusty debris disk imaged by Hubble. Fomalhaut b, once thought to be an exoplanet, is now believed to be an expanding dust cloud from a collisional event.

galactic.name: Pollux
galactic.desc: Brightest star in Gemini and the nearest giant star to the Sun. Hosts confirmed exoplanet Pollux b (Thestias), a hot Jupiter with 2.3 Jupiter masses.

galactic.name: Arcturus
galactic.desc: Brightest star in Boötes and the northern hemisphere. K-type red giant, ~25× solar radius. Metal-poor halo star on a retrograde orbit — likely a captured remnant from an ancient dwarf galaxy.

galactic.name: Capella
galactic.desc: Sixth-brightest star, brightest in Auriga. Spectroscopic binary of two G-type giants orbiting each other every 104 days. Both components have evolved off the main sequence.

galactic.name: Aldebaran
galactic.desc: "Eye of the Bull." K-type red giant, 44× solar radius. Not physically part of the Hyades cluster (much closer at ~150 ly).

galactic.name: Regulus
galactic.desc: "Little King" — the brightest star in Leo. Rapidly rotating (15.9 hr) hot B-dwarf; rotation flattens it significantly. Part of a 4-star system.

galactic.name: Spica
galactic.desc: Brightest star in Virgo. Spectroscopic binary of two hot B-stars so close (18 million km) they are tidally distorted into egg shapes. Spica A is a variable (β Cephei type).

galactic.name: Pleiades (M45)
galactic.desc: Iconic open cluster in Taurus. ~1,000 stars dominated by hot B-type blue giants. Age ~100 Myr.

galactic.name: Antares
galactic.desc: Heart of Scorpius. Massive red supergiant with ~700 R☉ — one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye. Like Betelgeuse, an imminent supernova candidate on stellar timescales.

galactic.name: Canopus
galactic.desc: Second-brightest star in the sky. F-type bright giant, much more luminous than its apparent magnitude suggests. Used as a navigation star by spacecraft. Part of the Carina constellation.

galactic.name: Betelgeuse
galactic.desc: Massive red supergiant in Orion. Among the largest known stars (~764 R☉). Supernova candidate. The 2019–2020 "Great Dimming" was caused by a mass ejection and dust condensation.

galactic.name: Rigel
galactic.desc: Brightest star in Orion. Blue-white supergiant, one of the most intrinsically luminous stars visible without a telescope (~120,000 L☉). Part of the Orion OB1 association.

galactic.name: Deneb
galactic.desc: Luminous blue-white supergiant at the tail of Cygnus. Despite being ~2,615 ly away, still one of the brightest in the sky (~196,000 L☉). Parallax remains contested (Gaia EDR3 with corrections vs. older Hipparcos).

galactic.name: Eta Carinae
galactic.desc: Hypergiant luminous blue variable — one of the most massive and luminous stars known (~5,000,000 L☉). Binary system. Experienced a "Great Eruption" in 1843 that briefly made it the second-brightest star. Hypernova/PISN candidate.

galactic.name: Westerlund 1
galactic.desc: The most massive compact young star cluster in the Milky Way. Contains over 100,000 stars including numerous Wolf-Rayet stars, OB supergiants, and LBVs. Home to one of the largest known stars, Westerlund 1-26.

galactic.name: Omega Centauri (NGC 5139)
galactic.desc: Largest and most massive globular cluster in the Milky Way. ~10 million stars in a sphere 150 ly across. Likely the stripped core of an ancient dwarf galaxy. Contains a possible intermediate-mass black hole (~40,000 M☉).

galactic.name: 47 Tucanae (NGC 104)
galactic.desc: Second-largest globular cluster. Located near the Small Magellanic Cloud in the sky, though physically unrelated. Rich in millisecond pulsars (~25 known) and exotic X-ray binaries.

galactic.name: M13 — Hercules Cluster
galactic.desc: The Great Globular Cluster in Hercules — the most prominent globular visible from the northern hemisphere. Target of the 1974 Arecibo Message broadcast. Contains ~300,000 stars.

galactic.name: Acrab (β Sco)
galactic.desc: A multiple system anchoring the northern pincer of Scorpius. The "Graffias" pair (β¹ + β²) is a stunning telescopic double. β¹ itself is at least a six-component system. Famously occulted by Jupiter in 1971 — a rare event that constrained Jupiter's atmospheric structure.

galactic.name: Dschubba (δ Sco)
galactic.desc: Arabic "the forehead" — once thought a typical B-type subgiant. In June 2000 it unexpectedly brightened by ~50% and developed a circumstellar gas disc, revealing itself as a fast-rotating Be-star binary. Has remained brighter and more variable than its historical baseline ever since.

galactic.name: Pi Scorpii (π Sco)
galactic.desc: A close spectroscopic eclipsing binary forming the southern pincer of Scorpius. The two B-type components orbit every 1.57 days; periodic dips of ~0.04 mag from partial eclipses make it a textbook example of a "near-contact" binary.

galactic.name: Sigma Scorpii (σ Sco)
galactic.desc: A quadruple system at the head-to-heart link of Scorpius. Member of the Upper Scorpius OB association — the nearest region of recent massive-star formation, 5–10 Myr old. β-Cephei pulsator with a 0.247-day period; helps calibrate pulsation distance scales.

galactic.name: Tau Scorpii (τ Sco)
galactic.desc: Surprisingly strong, complex magnetic field for a hot star — one of the very few O/B stars with a confirmed fossil dynamo. A young (~5 Myr) massive star in the Upper Sco association; its X-ray emission is anomalously bright, a probable consequence of magnetic confinement of the stellar wind.

galactic.name: Epsilon Scorpii (ε Sco)
galactic.desc: A nearby orange giant — closest bright star in the Scorpius asterism to the Sun. Has measurably depleted lithium, suggesting deep convective mixing as it crossed the giant branch. Possible solar-system planet host (one candidate confirmed 2008 — HD 151249 b, mass 7 M_J).

galactic.name: Mu Scorpii (μ Sco)
galactic.desc: A close double known as the "Cat's Eyes" of Scorpius (with ζ Sco). μ¹ is itself a 1.45-day eclipsing binary in which two B-type stars nearly touch; total mass 21 M☉.

galactic.name: Zeta Scorpii (ζ²)
galactic.desc: A foreground K-giant projected onto the much more distant ζ¹ — an extreme blue hypergiant ~6,000 ly away. The "Cat's Eyes" optical pair of Scorpius (with μ Sco) is actually two unrelated stars at very different distances.
props: ζ² = K4 III (ζ¹ behind = B1 Ia⁺)

galactic.name: Eta Scorpii (η Sco)
galactic.desc: A peculiar F-type subgiant — chemically anomalous, with enhanced silicon and strontium and depleted calcium ("Ap-like" abundances despite the cooler temperature). Member of the Sirius supercluster moving group.

galactic.name: Sargas (θ Sco)
galactic.desc: Sumerian "the Smiter" — second-brightest star in Scorpius and the bright knot at the tail's bend before the sting. A massive F-type bright giant just leaving the main sequence. Slowly variable in radial velocity, suggesting an undetected companion.

galactic.name: Iota₁ Scorpii (ι¹ Sco)
galactic.desc: A rare F-type yellow supergiant — among the most luminous F-type stars known (~30,000 L☉). Distant despite its naked-eye visibility. Likely transiting the Hertzsprung gap from blue-supergiant ancestor to red supergiant; will end as a Type II supernova within a few hundred thousand years.

galactic.name: Girtab (κ Sco)
galactic.desc: Sumerian "the Scorpion." A β Cephei-type pulsating variable in a 196-day eccentric binary orbit. Forms the bend at the end of the tail just before the stinger.

galactic.name: Shaula (λ Sco)
galactic.desc: Arabic "the raised tail" — the scorpion's sting. Visually the second-brightest star in Scorpius, just behind Antares. A triple system: a 5.95-day spectroscopic pair plus a wide pre-main-sequence companion. β Cephei pulsator with a 0.2137-day period.

galactic.name: Lesath (υ Sco)
galactic.desc: Forms the "false double" with Shaula at the scorpion's stinger — the two are unrelated in physical space (Lesath is in the foreground of the same line of sight) but together they look like the venomous tip of the sting. Member of the Upper Scorpius OB association.

galactic.name: Cursa (β Eri)
galactic.desc: Arabic "the chair" — the northern end of the river Eridanus, just NW of Rigel in Orion. Rare cause of an unexplained 1985 brightening (~0.4 mag) lasting hours, the cause of which has never been firmly identified (planetary occultation or flare are the leading hypotheses).

galactic.name: Zaurak (γ Eri)
galactic.desc: Arabic "the boat." A semi-regular variable red giant — slow brightness oscillations of ~0.2 mag over ~57 days. Notable for its strong technetium absorption, suggesting it may be on or near the AGB.

galactic.name: Rana (δ Eri)
galactic.desc: A bright nearby subgiant — one of the closest "post-main-sequence" stars. A common asteroseismology target (CoRoT and TESS) because its solar-like oscillations and well-determined parallax let astronomers test stellar models with high precision.

galactic.name: Azha (η Eri)
galactic.desc: Persian "the ostrich nest." An evolved K-giant slightly past first dredge-up; mildly enhanced in CN and Na. Often used to mark the eastern bend of the river before it heads south.

galactic.name: Acamar (θ Eri)
galactic.desc: Arabic "the end of the river." Before precession lowered Achernar into view, Acamar was the southernmost point of Eridanus visible from the ancient Mediterranean — the actual "river's end." A stunning visual binary, two A-type stars separated by ~8.3″.

galactic.name: Achernar (α Eri)
galactic.desc: Arabic "the river's end" — the modern southernmost point of Eridanus and the ninth-brightest star in the sky. The most oblate star ever observed: its equatorial radius is ~50% larger than its polar radius, the result of an extreme ~250 km/s equatorial rotation (~88% of break-up).

galactic.name: V404 Cygni
galactic.desc: Recurrent black-hole microquasar — quiescent most of the time but produces spectacular outbursts when accretion-disk material avalanches onto the BH.  The June 2015 eruption was the brightest stellar-BH X-ray event in 26 years, briefly making it the brightest X-ray source in the sky and triggering a worldwide multi-wavelength campaign.

galactic.name: A0620-00 (V616 Mon)
galactic.desc: The best-measured stellar-mass black hole — its 6.6 M☉ has uncertainty of just ±0.25 M☉ thanks to the favourable 40° orbital inclination and short 7.75-hr period.  First detected as Nova Mon 1975 outburst, then quiescent for nearly 50 years.  The benchmark system for stellar-BH mass-function studies.

galactic.name: GRO J1655-40
galactic.desc: A prototypical microquasar — a stellar-mass BH producing relativistic radio jets at v ≈ 0.92c, scaled-down analogues of those from supermassive AGN.  Detected by the Compton GRO observatory in 1994; subsequent outbursts (1996, 2005) revealed an iron-line wind from the inner accretion disk.  Used to test GR Lense-Thirring frame-dragging via its quasi-periodic oscillations.

galactic.name: GRS 1915+105
galactic.desc: The fastest-spinning known black hole (a* > 0.98 — near the Kerr extremal bound) and the source of the longest X-ray outburst in history: continuously bright from 1992 until 2018, when it abruptly dimmed.  Hosted the first Galactic detection of apparent superluminal motion (1994); its radio jets reach v ≈ 0.98 c.

galactic.name: Orion Nebula (M42)
galactic.desc: The closest large region of massive star formation. A blister H II region carved out of the Orion Molecular Cloud by the radiation of the central Trapezium cluster (θ¹ Orionis). Visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword. The Hubble Space Telescope and JWST have catalogued thousands of protoplanetary disks ("proplyds") in its core.

galactic.name: Crab Nebula (M1)
galactic.desc: Remnant of supernova SN 1054, recorded by Chinese, Arab and Native-American astronomers in July 1054. Powered by the Crab Pulsar (PSR B0531+21) — a 33-ms-period neutron star whose relativistic wind inflates an expanding bubble of synchrotron-emitting plasma. The first object linked to a historical SN and the prototype pulsar wind nebula.
props: Pulsar Wind Nebula / Type II SNR
PSR B0531+21 — period 33.5 ms, B ~ 4×10¹² G

galactic.name: Eagle Nebula (M16) — Pillars of Creation
galactic.desc: A young (~2 Myr) star-forming region anchored by the open cluster NGC 6611. Famous for the "Pillars of Creation" — towers of dense molecular gas being slowly evaporated by ultraviolet radiation from O-stars in the cluster, with embedded "Evaporating Gaseous Globules" (EGGs) collapsing into new stars. Iconic targets for both Hubble (1995) and JWST (2022).
props: H II region + dark molecular pillars

galactic.name: Carina Nebula (NGC 3372)
galactic.desc: One of the largest diffuse nebulae in the sky — a vast complex of glowing gas and dark dust ~460 ly across, four times larger than the Orion Nebula. Houses several massive young clusters (Trumpler 14, 16) and an exceptional sample of LBVs and Wolf-Rayet stars, including the famously unstable η Carinae. JWST's "Cosmic Cliffs" image (2022) shows its NGC 3324 ionization edge.

galactic.name: Eta Carinae (η Car)
galactic.desc: A luminous blue variable binary at the heart of the Carina Nebula, comprising the most luminous star known in our Galaxy (~5 million L☉) and a hot evolved companion. Underwent the "Great Eruption" of 1843 — briefly the second-brightest star in the sky — ejecting the bipolar Homunculus Nebula now expanding at ~650 km/s. Considered an imminent (geologically speaking) supernova candidate.

galactic.name: Cassiopeia A
galactic.desc: The youngest known supernova remnant in our Galaxy — its progenitor exploded around 1670 CE (light first reached Earth then), but no clear historical sighting was recorded, suggesting heavy interstellar extinction. Brightest extrasolar radio source in the sky (Cas A = 3C 461). The first object whose forward shock has been imaged in light-echo "movies"; JWST detail (2023) revealed unprecedented ejecta filaments.
props: Type IIb SN remnant + central compact object

galactic.name: Helix Nebula (NGC 7293) — "Eye of God"
galactic.desc: The closest planetary nebula to Earth and a textbook example of late-stage stellar death. Its central white dwarf (WD 2226-210) ionises a slowly-expanding shell of gas shed by the progenitor red giant ~10,500 years ago. Hubble revealed ~40,000 "cometary knots" — dense globules of gas with comet-like tails — embedded in the shell. Often nicknamed the "Eye of God."
props: ~2.87 ly main ring (~6 ly with halo)

galactic.name: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868)
galactic.desc: The first object ever widely accepted as a black hole (Webster & Murdin / Bolton 1971). A 21 M☉ stellar-mass BH accretes from the ~40 M☉ supergiant HDE 226868 in a 5.6-day orbit. Persistent X-ray emission from the inner accretion disk and a faint relativistic jet inflate a ~25-ly radio nebula in the surrounding ISM. The 1974 Hawking–Thorne wager was settled in 1990 in favour of "yes, it's a black hole."

galactic.name: WR 104 — "Pinwheel"
galactic.desc: A binary system whose Wolf-Rayet primary (WC9) and OB companion drive colliding stellar winds that condense dust into a brilliant Archimedean-spiral "pinwheel," first imaged with the Keck aperture-masking interferometer (Tuthill et al. 1999). The pinwheel rotates with the 220-day orbit. Its rotation axis appears to point near Earth — fueling debate over whether it could deliver a long GRB if the system goes supernova, though more recent measurements suggest the axis is misaligned.
props: Keck aperture masking — Tuthill et al. 1999

galactic.name: Vela Pulsar + Vela SNR (PSR B0833-45)
galactic.desc: A young (~11,400-yr) glitching pulsar embedded in its own ~110-ly supernova remnant. The 89 ms pulsar drives a Chandra-imaged X-ray jet and pulsar wind nebula. Periodic "glitches" — sudden spin-up events — make it a key target for neutron-star superfluid physics. The host SNR is the closest large supernova remnant to Earth.

galactic.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
galactic.desc: Largest satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Visible to the naked eye from the southern hemisphere. Hosts the Tarantula Nebula — the most active star-forming region in the Local Group. Destined to merge with the Milky Way in ~2.4 Gyr.

galactic.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
galactic.desc: Second-largest satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Contains ~3 billion stars. Connected to the LMC via the Magellanic Bridge (a stream of gas). Used historically for measuring cosmic distances via Cepheid variables.

galactic.name: Fornax Dwarf Spheroidal
galactic.desc: One of the most luminous Milky Way satellite dwarfs. Hosts six globular clusters — an unusual richness for so small a system — and shows multiple stellar populations spanning ~10 Gyr of star formation, suggesting it has a complex chemical history. Heavily dark-matter dominated.

galactic.name: Sculptor Dwarf Spheroidal
galactic.desc: The first dwarf galaxy ever discovered (Shapley, 1938). A tiny spherical clump of ancient (~13 Gyr) metal-poor stars at the south galactic pole. Heavily dominated by dark matter. The progenitor of much of the southern halo stellar inventory.

galactic.name: Draco Dwarf Spheroidal
galactic.desc: A textbook ultra-faint dwarf with one of the highest mass-to-light ratios known (~440), making it a key target for indirect dark matter searches (γ-ray, neutrino). Star formation effectively shut off ~10 Gyr ago.

galactic.name: Leo I Dwarf Spheroidal
galactic.desc: The most distant of the "classical" Milky Way dwarf spheroidals — at ~820 kly, near the Local Group escape velocity. Recent kinematic studies hint at an unusually massive (~3 × 10⁶ M☉) central black hole relative to its tiny stellar mass.

galactic.name: Antlia 2 Dwarf
galactic.desc: A "ghostly" ultra-low-surface-brightness dwarf discovered in Gaia DR2 (Torrealba+ 2019). At ~12,000 ly across it rivals the Large Magellanic Cloud in size yet is 10,000× fainter. Its trajectory may have created a long-suspected dark-matter perturbation in the Milky Way disk.
props: Possible cause of MW disk DM-perturbation

galactic.name: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
galactic.desc: The nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way. Slightly larger than our galaxy with ~1 trillion stars. Approaching at ~110 km/s — on a collision course. The Milky Way–Andromeda merger is expected in ~4.5 Gyr, forming "Milkomeda."

galactic.name: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
galactic.desc: Third-largest galaxy in the Local Group. A loosely wound spiral with very little bulge. Home to the giant H II region NGC 604, one of the largest known star-forming nebulae (1,500 ly across).
props: NGC 604 — giant H II region (1,500 ly)

galactic.name: M87 (Virgo A)
galactic.desc: Massive elliptical galaxy at the core of the Virgo Cluster. Hosts M87* — the first black hole ever directly imaged (Event Horizon Telescope, April 2019). Drives a 5,000 ly relativistic jet at near-light speed.

galactic.name: Phoenix Cluster (SPT-CL J2344−4243)
galactic.desc: The most X-ray luminous galaxy cluster known and one of the most massive structures in the observable universe. Named for its remarkable "phoenix-like" cooling flow: the central BCG is forming stars at ~800 M☉/yr — the highest rate in any known cluster. Discovered by the South Pole Telescope (2010). At z=0.596, its light left when the universe was 7.7 Gyr old.
props: ~2.5 × 10¹⁵ M☉ (one of the most massive known)

galactic.name: 3C 273
galactic.desc: The first quasar ever identified (1963) and one of the brightest in the sky at mag 12.9 — visible in amateur telescopes. Located ~2.05 Gly (light-travel) away yet bright enough to have been first mistaken for a nearby star. Drives a one-sided relativistic jet ~200,000 ly long.
props: 2.05 Gly light-travel · 2.4 Gly luminosity (749 Mpc D_L)

galactic.name: APM 08279+5255
galactic.desc: One of the most luminous and distant known quasars at redshift z=3.91 — its light left when the universe was only 1.8 billion years old. The central black hole is estimated at ~23 billion M☉. So bright it was initially mistaken for a nearby brown dwarf.

galactic.name: Ton 618
galactic.desc: One of the most massive black holes known — ~66 billion M☉. A hyperluminous quasar at redshift z=2.219, meaning its light left when the universe was only ~3 billion years old. Powered an AGN so bright it was originally catalogued as a star.

galactic.name: NGC 4889 (Coma B)
galactic.desc: A giant cD elliptical anchoring the Coma Cluster core (with NGC 4874).  Hosts one of the largest known black holes — ~21 billion M☉, comparable to Ton 618 but in the local universe.  The first SMBH whose mass was measured via stellar-velocity dispersion alone, requiring the M-σ relation to be extrapolated to extreme regimes.
props: Coma — one of the two giant cDs
Among largest known SMBHs in the local universe

galactic.name: OJ 287 (Binary SMBH)
galactic.desc: A BL Lac blazar harbouring the best-confirmed binary supermassive black hole system.  The primary BH (~18.3 billion M☉) is orbited by a secondary (~150 million M☉) every ~12 years — and the secondary punches through the primary's accretion disk twice per orbit, producing predictable optical outbursts (1971, 1983, 1995, 2007, 2015, 2019 …).  The 2019 flare confirmed general-relativistic precession of the orbit.

galactic.name: GW150914 (First BH-BH merger)
galactic.desc: The first direct detection of gravitational waves — 14 Sep 2015, 09:50:45 UTC, by LIGO Hanford + Livingston.  Two stellar-mass black holes (~36 + 29 M☉) spiralled together and merged, radiating ~3 M☉ of mass-energy as gravitational waves in ~0.2 s — momentarily outpowering the combined electromagnetic luminosity of every star in the observable universe.  Nobel Prize 2017.

galactic.name: GW190521 (First IMBH)
galactic.desc: The most massive black-hole merger detected to date — 21 May 2019 by LIGO/Virgo.  The 85-M☉ primary sits squarely in the pair-instability supernova mass gap (~65–135 M☉), where stellar collapse should not be able to form a BH directly — strongly suggesting it formed from an earlier merger.  The 142-M☉ remnant is the first direct detection of an intermediate-mass black hole.

galactic.name: Centaurus A (NGC 5128)
galactic.desc: The closest active galactic nucleus to Earth and the fifth-brightest galaxy in the sky. A peculiar lenticular galaxy bisected by a dramatic dust lane — the result of an ancient merger with a spiral galaxy. Drives a 1.4-million-light-year-long radio jet visible from Earth.
props: Closest AGN; merger remnant with prominent dust lane

galactic.name: M82 (Cigar Galaxy)
galactic.desc: A prototypical edge-on starburst galaxy with star-formation rates ~10× the Milky Way. Tidal interaction with M81 funnelled gas into the core, igniting a "superwind" of hot gas blowing perpendicular to the disk that is visible in Hα and X-ray imagery.

galactic.name: M81 (Bode’s Galaxy / NGC 3031)
galactic.desc: A grand-design spiral and the brightest member of the M81 Group. Its sweeping symmetric arms — sharpened by interaction with M82 and NGC 3077 — make it one of the most photogenic galaxies in the northern sky. Contains a low-luminosity AGN powered by a ~7 × 10⁷ M☉ black hole.
props: Brightest member of the M81 Group

galactic.name: NGC 253 (Sculptor Galaxy)
galactic.desc: The largest member of the Sculptor Group and one of the closest starburst galaxies. An intermediate spiral seen nearly edge-on, with a vigorously star-forming nucleus and clumpy dust lanes. Notable for its galactic-scale outflow detected in X-ray and millimetre wavelengths.

galactic.name: M51 (Whirlpool Galaxy)
galactic.desc: The first galaxy ever recognised as a spiral (Lord Rosse, 1845). Two interacting galaxies — NGC 5194 and the smaller NGC 5195 — locked in a tidal embrace that has sharpened M51’s magnificent two-arm structure. A modern textbook example of grand-design spiral morphology.

galactic.name: M104 (Sombrero Galaxy)
galactic.desc: Hat-shaped galaxy famous for its bright bulge, prominent edge-on dust lane, and unusually large supermassive black hole (~10⁹ M☉). Its halo of hundreds of globular clusters and intermediate-age stellar population suggest a complex, possibly merger-driven, formation history.
props: ~1 × 10⁹ M☉ (one of the largest in the local universe)

galactic.name: Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038/4039)
galactic.desc: A canonical late-stage major merger between two formerly separate spiral galaxies. Shock-compressed gas has triggered an extreme starburst — including hundreds of newly forming "super star clusters" — visible across the optical, IR and X-ray bands. The trailing tidal tails give the system its name.

galactic.name: NGC 6240
galactic.desc: Late-stage galaxy merger hosting two — and possibly three — supermassive black holes separated by only ~3,000 ly. An ultraluminous infrared galaxy (ULIRG) with shocked molecular gas, intense star formation, and X-ray luminous AGN signatures. A nearby analog of the merger-driven AGN activity that dominated the early universe.
props: Possibly a third lurking SMBH; merger analogue for early universe

galactic.name: TXS 0506+056
galactic.desc: The first astrophysical source confidently associated with a high-energy neutrino. On 22 Sept 2017, IceCube detected a 290-TeV neutrino spatially coincident with this blazar during a multi-wavelength flare — opening multi-messenger astronomy with neutrinos and pinpointing blazars as long-suspected cosmic accelerators.
props: Fermi-LAT γ-ray flare during neutrino arrival

galactic.name: J0529-4351 (Most Luminous Quasar)
galactic.desc: The most luminous object known in the universe (Onken et al., Nature Astronomy, Feb 2024). At redshift z=3.962, this quasar shines with 500 trillion times the luminosity of the Sun — fueled by a supermassive black hole accreting an entire Sun’s worth of mass per day. Its accretion disk alone is ~7 light-years across.
props: Onken et al. 2024 — eROSITA + Siding Spring confirmation

galactic.name: Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal
galactic.desc: A dwarf spheroidal galaxy on the opposite side of the galactic centre from us, currently being torn apart by Milky Way tides. Its stripped stars form the Sagittarius Stream — a vast tidal arc looping over our galactic poles — used as a sensitive probe of the Milky Way’s dark matter halo.
props: Probe of MW dark matter potential

galactic.name: MoM-z14 (CAPERS-LRD-z14)
galactic.desc: Candidate for most-distant spectroscopically confirmed object — light left when the universe was only ~280 Myr old. A "Little Red Dot" (LRD): an extraordinarily compact, red, point-like source whose nature (compact star-forming galaxy or accreting massive seed black hole) is still being debated. Submitted June 2025 (Naidu et al.) from the COSMOS-Web/CAPERS programmes.
props: JWST CAPERS / COSMOS-Web — Naidu et al. 2025
Possibly displaces JADES-GS-z14-0 from the record

galactic.name: JADES-GS-z14-0
galactic.desc: Most distant spectroscopically confirmed object known. Light left this galaxy when the universe was only ~290 million years old. JWST NIRSpec confirmation announced May 2024 (Carniani et al.). Surprisingly luminous and ~1,600 ly across — challenging models of early galaxy formation.

galactic.name: JADES-GS-z14-1
galactic.desc: Companion record-holder confirmed alongside JADES-GS-z14-0 in the same JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey paper. Light left when the universe was ~310 Myr old. Smaller and fainter than its sibling but still spectroscopically secure via Lyman-α break.

galactic.name: HD1
galactic.desc: Candidate for the most-distant galaxy at the time of its 2022 announcement (Harikane et al.) — photometrically placed at z ≈ 13.27 from a 1,200-hr Subaru/HSC + VISTA + Spitzer search. ALMA tentative [O III] line set z ≈ 13.27. Star-forming rate (~110 M☉/yr) so high it has been suggested to host a Population III starburst or a 10⁷ M☉ direct-collapse seed black hole. Spectroscopic confirmation remains contested.

galactic.name: JADES-GS-z13-0
galactic.desc: First JADES galaxy spectroscopically confirmed beyond z=13. Light left when the universe was ~330 Myr old. Set the redshift record from December 2022 until JADES-GS-z14-0 surpassed it in May 2024.

galactic.name: GHZ2 (GLASS-z12)
galactic.desc: Extraordinarily compact primordial galaxy lensed by the Abell 2744 ("Pandora") cluster. Spectroscopy revealed unusually strong nitrogen-to-carbon ratios — possible signature of a runaway-collapse super-massive star or globular-cluster precursor. Universe was ~360 Myr old at emission.
props: JWST GLASS / NIRCam — Castellano et al. 2022

galactic.name: JADES-GS-z11-0
galactic.desc: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopic confirmation of a Lyman-α drop-out at z ≈ 11.58 in the GOODS-S/JADES field. A surprisingly mature stellar population for the cosmic age (~410 Myr) — suggesting earlier formation in the universe's first 200 Myr. Compact (~620 ly), with a stellar mass already approaching 10⁹ M☉.

galactic.name: GN-z11
galactic.desc: Held the spectroscopic redshift record from 2016 to 2022 (Hubble grism), reconfirmed by JWST in 2024. Surprisingly luminous — ~25× more massive than expected at its epoch. Hosts an active galactic nucleus suggesting an early supermassive black hole seed.
props: Hubble WFC3 grism — Oesch et al. 2016

galactic.name: MACS0647-JD
galactic.desc: Gravitationally lensed by the MACS J0647+7015 galaxy cluster into three separate images of the same galaxy. JWST NIRCam (2022) revealed it as two merging components — the earliest galaxy merger ever observed. Lensing magnification ~8×.

galactic.name: MACS1149-JD1
galactic.desc: ALMA detection of doubly-ionised oxygen ([O III] 88 µm) provided indirect evidence of star formation as early as z≈15 — meaning some of its stars formed when the universe was only ~250 Myr old. JWST has since resolved the galaxy and confirmed the ancient stellar population.

galactic.name: EGSY8p7
galactic.desc: Held the spectroscopic redshift record (z = 8.683) from 2015 to 2016. Notable for showing strong Lyman-α emission despite sitting deep in the era of Reionization — implying an unusually large ionised "bubble" had already opened around it, allowing the photons to escape. Located in the Extended Groth Strip (EGS) survey field.

galactic.name: GRB 090423
galactic.desc: Most distant gamma-ray burst ever observed. Triggered NASA Swift on 23 April 2009. The collapse of a primordial massive star released ~10⁵² erg of gamma rays — briefly outshining its entire host galaxy. The afterglow let astronomers probe the early-universe interstellar medium.

galactic.name: J0313-1806
galactic.desc: Most distant quasar known. Hosts a 1.6-billion-M☉ supermassive black hole already in place when the universe was only ~670 Myr old — a profound challenge to standard BH growth models. Drives a fast (~20 % c) ionised wind, evidence of ongoing super-Eddington accretion.

galactic.name: ULAS J1342+0928
galactic.desc: Held the most-distant-quasar record from 2017 to 2021 (until J0313-1806). An ~800 million M☉ supermassive black hole already in place when the universe was only ~690 Myr old — a profound challenge to standard accretion-rate models. Its spectrum reveals a surprisingly large neutral-hydrogen fraction along the line of sight, pinpointing the tail end of cosmic reionisation.

galactic.name: GN-108036
galactic.desc: Held the spectroscopic redshift record (z = 7.213) from 2010 to 2012. Discovered in the GOODS-N deep field with Hubble + Spitzer photometry, then confirmed via a Lyman-α line at Subaru. Its star-formation rate (~30 M☉/yr) is unusually vigorous for its modest stellar mass, an early hint at "burstier" early-universe galaxy growth.

galactic.name: Earendel (WHL0137-LS)
galactic.desc: Most distant individual star ever resolved. Discovered by Hubble (2022) and confirmed by JWST (2023). Lensed by the WHL0137-08 galaxy cluster onto a "lensing critical curve" that magnifies it by a factor of thousands. Likely a massive (>50 M☉) hot blue B-type star or close binary in an early host galaxy nicknamed the "Sunrise Arc."
props: Most distant individual star ever resolved

galactic.name: Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall
galactic.desc: The largest known structure in the observable universe — a filamentary overdensity of long-duration gamma-ray-burst host galaxies stretching ~10 Gly across the Hercules / Corona Borealis sky. Its existence (Horváth, Bagoly & Tóth 2014) tests the cosmological principle: at this scale, the universe is supposed to be smooth, yet here is a coherent feature ~10% the size of the observable universe itself.

galactic.name: Huge-LQG (Large Quasar Group)
galactic.desc: A coherent filament of 73 quasars at z ≈ 1.27, spanning ~4 Gly along its longest axis (Clowes et al. 2013). Its discovery in SDSS DR7Q briefly held the title of "largest known structure" until being eclipsed by the Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall. Statistically inconsistent with the homogeneity scale predicted by ΛCDM (~370 Mpc) — still actively debated.

galactic.name: Sloan Great Wall
galactic.desc: A wall-like sheet of galaxy clusters and superclusters identified in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (Gott et al. 2005). At ~1.4 Gly long it was the largest known structure in the universe at its discovery. Sits roughly in the same direction as Virgo / Coma but ~3× more distant. Comprises several rich clusters bound by an ~80 Mpc-thick filament.

galactic.name: Saraswati Supercluster
galactic.desc: One of the most massive supercluster structures known (~2 × 10¹⁶ M☉, ~600 Mly across) at the high-z (z ≈ 0.28) era of cosmic acceleration. Its discovery (Bagchi et al. 2017) shows that very-large-mass clusters were already in place when dark energy began to dominate cosmic dynamics — pushing the lower bound on supercluster formation timescales.

galactic.name: Laniakea Supercluster
galactic.desc: The supercluster the Milky Way actually belongs to — defined dynamically (Tully et al. 2014) as the basin of attraction of the Great Attractor. Contains ~100,000 galaxies organised into the Virgo, Hydra-Centaurus, Pavo-Indus and Norma sub-superclusters. We sit on its periphery and are flowing inward at ~600 km/s.
props: The Milky Way is on its outskirts

galactic.name: Boötes Void
galactic.desc: A roughly spherical region of the universe ~330 Mly across that contains essentially no galaxies — fewer than 60 known where ~10,000 are expected. Discovered serendipitously by Kirshner et al. 1981 in a redshift survey of the constellation Boötes. The largest known void; its existence places strong constraints on the initial power spectrum of cosmic structure.

galactic.name: Great Attractor (Norma Cluster region)
galactic.desc: A gravitational focal point pulling the Local Group at ~600 km/s toward the constellation Norma. Centred near the Norma Cluster (Abell 3627), its density is ~10× the cosmic mean. Largely hidden behind the Milky Way's "Zone of Avoidance" — its existence was first inferred from the dipole anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background.
props: Hidden behind Milky Way Zone of Avoidance

galactic.name: Coma Cluster (Abell 1656)
galactic.desc: One of the densest known galaxy clusters — ~1,000 identified members plus thousands of dwarfs. Historically pivotal: Fritz Zwicky's 1933 study of its galaxy velocity dispersion produced the first quantitative evidence for dark matter. Two giant cD galaxies (NGC 4874 and NGC 4889) anchor its core. Hot intracluster gas at ~10⁸ K dominates its X-ray sky.

galactic.name: IC 1101
galactic.desc: Among the largest single galaxies known — a supergiant cD elliptical at the centre of the Abell 2029 cluster. Its diffuse stellar envelope spans ~6 million light-years (~50× the Milky Way), although ~75% of that "size" is intracluster light. Hosts a ~4 × 10¹⁰ M☉ central black hole and ~100 trillion stars.
props: One of the largest known galaxies

galactic.name: Stephan's Quintet (HCG 92)
galactic.desc: A compact group of five galaxies (four interacting at ~290 Mly + one foreground member at 39 Mly) showcasing one of the most violent ongoing intergalactic collisions. Featured in JWST's 2022 first-light imagery; the intruder NGC 7318B is plowing into the group at ~1,000 km/s, generating a galaxy-scale shock wave detected from radio through X-ray.
